title: Valid Palindrome
description: Brute force to optimized: building a cleaned copy of the string versus a two-pointer scan that skips non-alphanumeric characters in place.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement
Problem Summary: Given a string s, determine whether it reads the same forwards and backwards after removing every character that is not a letter or digit, and ignoring uppercase versus lowercase.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Detail"],"rows":[["Pattern","Two pointers converging from both ends of a sequence to check for symmetry, skipping over characters that do not participate in the comparison."],["Difficulty","Beginner"],["Tags","Strings, Two Pointers"],["Interview Focus","Recognizing that a symmetry check never needs a full cleaned copy of the data, comparing directly from both ends inward is enough."]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem
Given a string s, determine whether it reads the same forwards and backwards after removing every character that is not a letter or digit, and ignoring uppercase versus lowercase.

blocks.title: Analogy: Reading a Noisy Sign Both Ways
blocks.text: Picture a weathered street sign with punctuation marks and smudges scattered across it, and imagine reading only the actual letters and numbers off that sign, ignoring every smudge and every difference between capital and lowercase. The question is simply whether that cleaned up reading looks the same whether read left to right or right to left.

blocks.caption: Keep only letters and digits, ignore case, then check for a palindrome

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: s = "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama"

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result"],"rows":[["Keep only letters and digits, lowercased","\"amanaplanacanalpanama\""],["Is it the same forwards and backwards?","Yes"]]}

blocks.text: The cleaned string reads the same in both directions, so the answer is true.
Example: s = "race a car"

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result"],"rows":[["Keep only letters and digits, lowercased","\"raceacar\""],["Is it the same forwards and backwards?","No"]]}

blocks.text: The cleaned string does not match its own reverse, so the answer is false.
Edge case: s = " "
After removing the single space, nothing is left at all. An empty string is considered a palindrome, so the answer is true.
5. How Should We Think?
Before writing any code, it helps to ask exactly how much of the string actually needs to exist as a separate, cleaned copy in memory.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: This is fundamentally a symmetry check, does the sequence look the same read from the front as it does read from the back, the same kind of question asked about any palindrome.

Observation 2: Checking symmetry does not require the whole cleaned sequence to exist at once, it only ever requires comparing one character from the front against one character from the back, at a time.

Observation 3: Since non alphanumeric characters do not count toward the comparison at all, they can simply be skipped over as they are encountered, rather than being filtered out into a separate copy beforehand.

Observation 4: Two pointers, one starting at each end and moving inward, naturally combine both of these ideas, skip past anything irrelevant, then compare, without ever materializing a cleaned copy of the string.
That reasoning is what turns "build a cleaned string, then check it" into "check directly, skipping the irrelevant characters as you go".
6. Brute Force Solution

Scan through the string once, keeping only the letters and digits and converting each one to lowercase, building a brand new cleaned up string. Then simply compare that cleaned string to its own reverse.
Step by step algorithm

items: Loop through every character of the input string.
Keep the character only if it is a letter or a digit, converting it to lowercase.
Collect all the kept characters into a new, cleaned string.
Reverse that cleaned string and compare it to the original cleaned string.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: build a cleaned copy of the string, then compare it to its own reverse

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every character is tested and possibly lowercased in a single pass, building the cleaned string incrementally rather than filtering and casing it in two separate passes.
The cleaned string is built once and then reversed as a whole, so the comparison at the end is a single, simple equality check rather than a character by character loop written by hand.
Keeping the filtering, casing, and collection together in one loop makes it easy to see exactly which characters end up mattering for the palindrome check.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
This is correct, since the cleaned string contains exactly the characters that matter for the palindrome check, in the exact order they originally appeared.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), one pass to build the cleaned string, and comparing it to its reverse is also O(n).
Space: O(n), for the cleaned string, and another O(n) for its reversed copy.

Limitation: building an entirely new string, and then a reversed copy of it, uses extra memory that is not strictly necessary. The check can instead be done directly on the original string, by comparing characters from both ends and moving inward, without ever allocating a new copy.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why building a cleaned copy works but is wasteful: the cleaned string, and then its reversed copy, both need to be fully stored in memory, even though the check only ever compares two characters at a time.

What is actually needed at any single moment: just the next relevant character from the front and the next relevant character from the back, nothing more.

Can the irrelevant characters be handled without a separate cleaning pass: yes, a pointer can simply step past a non alphanumeric character in place, rather than that character ever being copied anywhere.

Can the comparison happen without ever building a full copy: yes, comparing the current front character to the current back character, ignoring case, is exactly the palindrome check, one pair at a time.

The core idea: two pointers starting at each end, each skipping past non alphanumeric characters before comparing, moving inward until they meet or a mismatch is found.

Use two pointers, one starting at the very beginning of the string and one at the very end. Skip past any character that is not a letter or digit on either side, then compare the two remaining letters, ignoring case. If they ever disagree, the string is not a palindrome. If the pointers meet in the middle without ever disagreeing, it is.
9. Optimized Solution
Two pointers start at opposite ends of the string and move inward, each skipping past any non alphanumeric character before every comparison.
Dry run for s = "race a car"

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Left character","Right character","Result","Why"],"rows":[["1","'r'","'r'","Match, move both pointers inward","Both are the first alphanumeric characters from their respective ends, no skipping needed yet."],["2","'a'","'a'","Match, move both pointers inward","Still no non alphanumeric characters encountered by either pointer."],["3","'c'","'c'","Match, move both pointers inward","Continuing inward with no skips needed so far."],["4","'e'","'a'","Mismatch, return false","'e' and 'a' disagree, so the function returns false here, before either pointer ever reaches the space in the middle of the string."]]}

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: two pointers converge inward, skipping non alphanumeric characters

blocks.text: Why This Works

This works because a palindrome check is symmetric by definition, the character at distance k from the front must equal the character at distance k from the back, for every valid k. Skipping non alphanumeric characters in place, rather than filtering them into a separate string first, does not change which characters get compared to which, it only changes where that filtering happens, directly inside the same pass that does the comparing.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What Happens","Result"],"rows":[["Both pointers land on alphanumeric characters that match, ignoring case","Both pointers move one step further inward","The check continues toward the middle of the string"],["A pointer lands on a non alphanumeric character","That pointer steps past it without any comparison","The comparison always happens between two genuinely relevant characters"],["Two alphanumeric characters disagree, ignoring case","The function returns false immediately","No further characters need to be examined once a genuine mismatch is found"],["The two pointers meet or cross without any mismatch","The loop ends naturally","The string is confirmed to be a palindrome, since every pair agreed"]]}

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), each character is visited at most once by either pointer.
Space: O(1) extra space, no copy of the string is ever created, this is the real floor for this problem, since every character must be examined at least once, and no extra memory beyond a couple of pointers is ever needed.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

The two pointer pattern is the natural fit whenever a problem asks whether something is symmetric, working inward from both ends avoids building any extra copy of the data, turning an O(n) space solution into an O(1) space one while keeping the same O(n) time.
Common Mistakes

items: Forgetting to ignore case when comparing characters, which would incorrectly reject strings like "Aa" as not a palindrome.
Not skipping non alphanumeric characters on both sides independently before comparing, which can misalign the two pointers.
Forgetting that an empty string, or a string with no letters or digits at all, should be treated as a palindrome.

blocks.text: Edge Cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["Empty string, or a string of only punctuation and spaces","Counts as a palindrome, since nothing remains to disagree with anything."],["A string of a single character","Always a palindrome, since there is nothing to compare it against."]]}

blocks.text: Interview Tips

Explicitly naming this as a two pointer problem, and pointing out that it avoids the extra space of building a cleaned copy, is a strong signal, this exact pattern reappears constantly in problems that check for symmetry in a sequence.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you avoid the extra copy", think: two pointers converging from both ends, skipping irrelevant characters in place.
If the interviewer says "what about punctuation and case", think: skip non alphanumeric characters and compare in lowercase, without ever building a separate cleaned string.
If the interviewer says "what should an empty result count as", think: an empty or fully filtered string is conventionally treated as a palindrome.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: Why does a symmetry check never actually require a full cleaned copy of the sequence in memory?
How would you adapt this two pointer approach to allow skipping at most one mismatched character, as in the follow-up "Valid Palindrome II" problem?
Can you check for a palindrome across a stream of characters where the full length is not known in advance?
How would this approach change if the definition of a valid character included underscores or other symbols?
How would you extend this technique to check whether a string is a palindrome after removing exactly one arbitrary character?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Any palindrome check on an array or string, where working inward from both ends is almost always at least as good as, and usually better than, building a reversed copy.
Two pointer problems on sorted arrays, which share the same converge-from-both-ends structure, even though the comparison condition differs.
String cleaning and filtering problems in general, where the same character can often be validated and used in a single pass instead of two.
The "Valid Palindrome II" follow-up problem, which reuses this exact two pointer skeleton with one added allowance for a single mismatch.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force approach runs in O(n) time and O(n) extra space, needing a cleaned copy and a reversed copy of the string. The two pointer approach also runs in O(n) time but only O(1) extra space, the real floor for this problem, since checking symmetry cannot avoid visiting every relevant character at least once.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: two pointers converging from both ends of a sequence to check for symmetry, skipping over characters that do not participate in the comparison.

Core Idea: a palindrome check never needs a fully cleaned copy of the string, comparing one relevant character from the front against one from the back at a time, while skipping irrelevant characters in place, is enough.
Time: O(n) for both the brute force and the optimized version.
Space: O(n) for the brute force, to hold the cleaned string and its reverse; O(1) extra for the optimized two pointer version.
Most Important Observation: checking symmetry is a streaming comparison, not a data transformation, so it rarely needs a full extra copy of the input.
Interview Difficulty: easy to write the brute force version; recognizing that skipping and comparing can happen in the very same pass is what shows real understanding.
One line memory trick: two pointers, skip non alphanumeric characters in place, compare in lowercase, meet in the middle.
